title: Spin lifetime anisotropy in graphene induced by the SiO2 interface
authors: Aron W. Cummings, Chunhao Guo, Andrew Grieder, Shihao Tu, Mayank Gupta, Junqing Xu, Juan Marmolejo-Tejada, Yuan Ping
abstract: Understanding how common dielectric substrates influence the spin transport properties of graphene is essential for advancing graphene-based spintronic technologies. Here we use a comprehensive set of numerical simulations to reveal how a SiO$_2$ substrate modifies the spin texture and governs spin relaxation in graphene. Using first-principles density matrix dynamics simulations, as well as tight-binding (TB) transport simulations, we quantify the effects of electron-phonon scattering, impurity scattering, and electrostatic disorder on the spin relaxation process. We find that a 2D SiO$_2$ substrate induces a predominantly Rashba-type helical spin texture in graphene, leading to a spin lifetime anisotropy of 1/2. Meanwhile, bulk SiO$_2$ breaks in-plane symmetry in graphene, leading to anisotropic in-plane and out-of-plane components in the spin texture, which we capture with a newly-developed TB model of graphene. Transport simulations under realistic disorder conditions reveal a spin lifetime anisotropy between 0.5 and 1, similar to what is seen in measurements of graphene spin valves on a SiO$_2$ substrate. Our results reveal a more complex picture of spin relaxation at the ubiquitous graphene/SiO$_2$ interface, beyond the standard Rashba model, providing critical insight for interpreting experiments and guiding substrate engineering for graphene spintronics.
summary: This paper uses advanced numerical simulations to investigate how SiO2 substrates modify spin transport in graphene. It finds that the interface dictates a complex spin texture, leading to measurable spin lifetime anisotropies depending on whether the substrate is modeled as 2D or bulk. The results offer critical guidance for interpreting experimental measurements and engineering better spintronic materials.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how common dielectric substrates, specifically SiO2, influence the spin transport properties of graphene for advancing spintronic technologies.
main_result: The substrate induces a complex spin texture beyond the standard Rashba model; 2D SiO2 yields $\zeta=1/2$, while bulk SiO2 leads to anisotropic relaxation ($\zeta > 1/2$), and oxygen vacancies show distinct EY-like behavior.
method: The research employs comprehensive numerical simulations, including first-principles density matrix dynamics (FPDMD) and tight-binding (TB) transport simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is graphene placed on SiO2 substrates (both 2D and bulk). The modeling incorporates Hamiltonian terms for nearest-neighbor hopping, Rashba SOC, electron-phonon scattering, impurity scattering, and electrostatic disorder.
key_observables: Spin texture, spin relaxation process, and the spin lifetime anisotropy ($\zeta = \tau_{s_z}/\tau_{s_x}$).
important_parameters: The substrate type (2D vs. bulk SiO2), scattering mechanisms (e-ph, impurity), and disorder strength are critical parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the standard Rashba model is insufficient to describe spin relaxation at this ubiquitous interface; approximations include using RTA for charge scattering in some analyses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures (2D vs. bulk SiO2), DFT band/spin textures, and scaling plots comparing spin relaxation rates and anisotropy ($\zeta$) under different conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical problem, detailing advanced simulation methods (FPDMD, TB modeling), presenting results for 2D and bulk substrates separately, analyzing specific scattering mechanisms (vacancies vs. disorder), and concluding with a comparative summary of the observed anisotropy.
why_interesting: This work provides detailed insights into spin relaxation in graphene interfaces, which is crucial for designing functional spintronic devices by understanding substrate-induced spin-orbit coupling effects beyond simple models.
